strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically important problem: attributing conditional distribution shift (concept shift) to a sparse set of interpretable features, going beyond existing work that either detects shift without diagnosis or focuses on covariate/marginal shift.

The proposed SGShift framework is well-motivated methodologically: it models the shift as a sparse GAM correction term on top of an existing (possibly black-box) source model, and cleanly extends with an absorption term for model misspecification and knockoffs for FDR/PFER-controlled feature selection.

The paper provides theoretical support, including a convergence guarantee for the penalized GAM estimator under restricted strong convexity and derandomized knockoff bounds extending existing PFER results to FDR control, adding some rigor beyond a purely empirical contribution.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three real healthcare datasets with multiple ML model classes (16 generator/base model combinations), with consistently large and robust improvements over constructed/adapted baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP) in AUC and recall, including in low target-sample-size regimes which is practically relevant.

A qualitative real-world case study (COVID-19 Omicron shift) shows the top selected features are broadly consistent with independent medical literature, lending some external validity to the method's outputs.
Reasonable reproducibility support: code, hyperparameters, and most datasets (or fetching scripts) provided in supplementary material and appendix.
weaknesses: The construction of basis functions ϕ(X) for the GAM is not clearly specified in the main text (e.g., what spline/basis family is used, how K relates to p, how coefficients map back to interpretable original features for nonlinear terms), which is important for both reproducibility and interpretability claims.

The semi-synthetic simulation protocol perturbs g(E[y|X]) via additive transformations of selected input features, which may align favorably with SGShift's own additive/sparse GAM inductive bias, potentially giving it a built-in advantage over baselines that do not share this functional form assumption; this raises concern about how representative the benchmark is of harder, non-additive real concept shifts.

The three baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP) are all self-constructed adaptations of methods designed for different tasks (regions of covariate space, unsupervised shift, etc.), rather than directly comparable published methods for this exact problem; while the paper notes no directly comparable prior method exists, the fairness and tuning quality of these adapted baselines is not clearly established.

The real-world validation (COVID-19 case study) is purely qualitative/narrative, relying on consistency with a handful of literature citations for a subset of top features, without any quantitative ground truth or statistical test of the substantive claims.

Theoretical contributions (Theorem 4.1, Lemma 4.2) are largely direct adaptations of standard high-dimensional lasso/RSC theory and existing derandomized knockoff PFER results, offering limited independent theoretical novelty beyond the specific offset/absorption setting.

Sensitivity of results to key hyperparameters (e.g., λω vs λδ ratio in the hierarchical regularization, number of knockoff realizations B, stability selection threshold π) is not empirically explored, leaving open how robust the method is to these choices in practice.

No discussion of computational cost/scalability of the knockoff-based derandomized procedure (which requires B knockoff realizations and repeated model fits), which could be a practical concern for larger feature sets or datasets.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: attributing concept shift (shift in p(y|X)) to a sparse set of specific features, rather than merely detecting that shift has occurred.

The modeling framework is clean and intuitive: using a GAM-based additive correction term on top of a black-box source model allows interpretable, feature-level attribution regardless of the base model's complexity.

Reasonably thorough set of theoretical results are provided, including a lasso-style estimation error bound under restricted strong convexity and derandomized knockoff-based FDR/PFER control, extending existing knockoff stability-selection guarantees to this differencing/offset setting.

Empirical evaluation spans three real healthcare datasets with semi-synthetic ground-truth shifted features, multiple model classes (16 generator/base combinations), varying sample sizes, and matched/mismatched model specification settings, giving reasonably broad coverage.

The real-data case study on COVID-19 severity shift around the Omicron variant produces a plausible, literature-consistent narrative (e.g., respiratory failure feature flipping sign), which is a nice qualitative validation of the method beyond the semi-synthetic benchmarks.
Code and preprocessing details (with exception of restricted-access COVID data) are provided, supporting reproducibility to a reasonable degree.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely a direct adaptation of standard lasso/GLM estimation-error theory (Theorem 4.1) and existing derandomized knockoff stability selection (Lemma 4.2, building essentially on [RWC23] and [CFJL18]) to this offset setting; the proofs closely mirror textbook arguments with limited new insight, and the novelty is incremental rather than foundational.

The real-data validation (Section 6, Figure 3) is purely qualitative and anecdotal—feature rankings are compared against informal consistency with cited medical literature, with no quantitative ground truth, statistical test, or inter-model agreement metric to substantiate that the selected shifted features are truly correct rather than plausible post-hoc narratives.

The baselines (Diff, WhyShift adaptation, SHAP adaptation) are self-constructed/adapted rather than being the original published implementations tuned by their authors for this exact task; this raises concern about whether the large performance gaps (AUC 0.1-0.2+ higher) partly reflect weak baseline tuning rather than genuine methodological superiority. No details are given on how baseline hyperparameters (e.g., tree depth for WhyShift, regression regularization for Diff) were selected or validated.

The semi-synthetic simulation design (fitting a generator to relabel source data, inducing an additive perturbation, then training a 'base' model) is somewhat circular with the SGShift framework itself—since the ground-truth shift is literally constructed as an additive transformation, the evaluation may favor SGShift's own modeling assumptions (additive, sparse basis function update) more than it would favor methods facing shifts that are nonadditive or non-sparse in reality; limited evidence is given for performance under shifts that violate SGShift's assumptions.

No comparison or discussion of computational cost/scalability (e.g., runtime for knockoff generation and stability selection with B realizations, especially combined with absorption terms and larger K), which matters for real-world adoption with larger feature sets.

The choice of basis functions ϕ(X) for the GAM component is not clearly specified or justified (linear terms? splines? how K relates to p for different feature types), making the method harder to reproduce exactly and raising questions about how continuous vs. categorical features are handled in the additive update.

The paper's claimed selection of hyperparameters (λ, λω, λδ, π, B) for knockoffs/absorption across experiments is not discussed in the main text, and sensitivity of results to these choices is not analyzed, which is important given the heavy reliance on regularization strength for the central AUC/recall results.

The discussion section is notably brief and does not substantively engage with limitations beyond a single sentence on dense shifts; issues such as model misspecification severity, violation of the sparsity assumption in practice, or failure modes of the absorption term are not explored.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: not just detecting distribution/concept shift, but attributing it to a sparse, interpretable set of features — a necessary step for actionable diagnosis and correction of model failures.

The core method (ℓ1-penalized GAM correction term) is simple, interpretable, and naturally composable with established statistical tools (lasso-style theory, Model-X knockoffs, stability selection), and the authors extend these tools non-trivially to the 'offset/correction' setting rather than simply citing prior results.

Solid theoretical contributions: a convergence guarantee for the estimation error of δ under RSC-type conditions adapted to the offset model, and new PFER/FDR control guarantees for a derandomized knockoff procedure applied to this correction-term setting.

Thoughtful methodological extensions: the absorption term (SGShift-A) explicitly addresses the realistic concern of poor source-model fit confounding shift detection, and hierarchical regularization (λω < λδ) is a sensible design choice to separate misspecification from true shift.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three real healthcare datasets with natural distribution shift, 16 generator/base model combinations per dataset, matched/mismatched model settings, and sample-size ablations, with full per-configuration results in the appendix — this is a notably thorough robustness check for a methods paper.

Consistently large and apparently robust performance gains over three carefully constructed/adapted baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP), including under model misspecification and at small target sample sizes, which is the realistic low-data regime practitioners would face.

The qualitative real-data case study (COVID-19 Omicron severity shift) cross-references the discovered top features against independent medical literature, lending some external validity beyond the semi-synthetic benchmarks.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: code provided, datasets largely public (with documented fetching procedure for the restricted All of Us data), and hyperparameters tabulated.
weaknesses: The ground-truth evaluation is entirely semi-synthetic (real covariates, simulated relabeling/shift); the only fully real-world assessment (COVID-19 Omicron) has no ground truth and relies on post-hoc, somewhat narrative matching to literature, so the central quantitative claims (AUC>0.9, recall>90%) are not verified on genuine real-world shifts.

Key practical details of basis-function construction (choice/number of GAM basis functions K, spline type, knot placement) are not clearly specified in the main text, which matters for both the theory (K enters the sample-complexity bound) and reproducibility; this is left vague relative to its importance.

No theoretical guarantees are given for the empirically best-performing variants that combine absorption with knockoffs (SGShift-A, SGShift-KA); the convergence theorem only covers plain SGShift, so the paper's strongest empirical claims are not backed by the stated theory.

The three baselines (Diff, WhyShift adaptation, SHAP adaptation) were constructed/adapted by the authors in the absence of directly comparable prior work; while reasonable given the literature gap, this raises some risk that the baselines are not fully optimized, which could inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

The structural assumption that the shift is an additive correction within the same basis/link as the source model (and that it is sparse in that basis) is fairly restrictive; shifts that involve nonlinear interactions, sign reversals not expressible in the chosen basis, or genuinely dense changes are acknowledged only briefly as a limitation rather than empirically stress-tested.

Computational cost and scalability (e.g., number of knockoff draws B, cost of stability selection, scaling to high-dimensional feature sets beyond ~30-65 features used here) are not discussed, leaving open how the method performs outside the tabular, moderate-dimensional healthcare setting studied.

The large confidence intervals noted when aggregating recall across model configurations (Figure 1) suggest substantial variance across model/generator pairings that is somewhat smoothed over in the main-text summary tables (Table 2), and the paper could more directly discuss cases where SGShift variants underperform (e.g., lower AUC with LR generator/base combinations in Table 4).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated reformulation of concept-shift diagnosis as sparse-correction estimation on top of a fixed source model, which elegantly avoids the error-accumulation problem of plugin approaches (fitting two separate conditional models and differencing them).

Three complementary variants (SGShift, SGShift-A for source misspecification, SGShift-K for FDR/PFER-controlled selection via knockoffs) give a coherent toolkit spanning point estimation, robustness to misspecification, and formal error control.

Reasonably rigorous theory: consistency results under standard high-dimensional M-estimation/RSC assumptions for both SGShift and SGShift-A, plus PFER and FDR control theorems for the knockoff variant, with proofs provided in the appendix.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 3 real healthcare datasets with natural concept shift, semi-synthetic simulations across 16 model combinations (base/generator mismatch), sparse vs. dense shift, sample-size sweeps, high-dimensional/correlated/low-SNR settings, global calibration shifts, and interaction-shift misspecification tests — this breadth substantially strengthens the empirical case.

Real-world case studies (COVID-19 respiratory failure feature, ancestry-specific Lupus genes) provide qualitative external validation against known clinical/biological findings, and the ACS Income sparsity-at-scale analysis (87 cases, all recoverable with <50% of features) supports the core sparse-update hypothesis.

Consistent and often large improvements over constructed/adapted baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP-based) across nearly all settings, with particularly notable robustness in high-dimensional and low-sample regimes where baselines collapse.
weaknesses: The main consistency theorem assumes the correction model is well-specified (g(E_T[Y|X]) = h_S(X) + φ(X)^Tδ*), which is a strong assumption unlikely to hold exactly in practice; the paper does not clearly quantify robustness to misspecification of this correction model itself (as opposed to misspecification of h_S, addressed by SGShift-A).

The penalty-calibration heuristic in Appendix F relies on an orthogonal-design, homoskedastic working approximation that is explicitly flagged as a simplification, yet this is the practical rule used for choosing λ in real applications; its reliability under realistic correlated designs is not empirically validated as carefully as the AUC/recall-based ranking evaluations.

Empirical FDR/power results for SGShift-K in Appendix E show meaningful FDR inflation (up to 0.11-0.15) and low power (as low as 0.21-0.42) in the Diabetes dataset, suggesting the formal guarantees are fragile in some realistic settings not fully discussed in the main text.

Baselines (Diff, adapted SHAP, WhyShift) are largely repurposed or self-constructed rather than being methods explicitly designed for this exact feature-level concept-shift attribution task, which may make the performance gap look larger than it would against a stronger tailored baseline.

Real-data validation of feature attributions (COVID-19, Lupus case studies) is qualitative/narrative, relying on consistency with prior literature rather than any ground-truth or quantitative validation, limiting the strength of claims about correctness of discovered shifted features in real settings.

Limited discussion of computational scalability beyond 500 features and no wall-clock/complexity analysis for the knockoff-based procedure with repeated draws, which could be a practical bottleneck for larger tabular datasets.

The paper's discussion section and impact statement are fairly brief and do not substantively discuss limitations of the sparsity assumption in real applications beyond the dense-shift simulation, nor potential harms of misattributing shifted features (e.g., in the ancestry/genetics case study, incorrect feature attributions could have sensitive implications).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: attributing conditional-distribution (concept) shift to a sparse, interpretable set of features without requiring a prespecified causal graph.

The core reformulation -- learning a sparse correction to a fixed source model rather than fitting and differencing two separately-estimated conditional means -- is a sensible way to avoid error accumulation from the 'plugin' approach used by prior work (e.g., WhyShift), and is reasonably well motivated.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 48 semi-synthetic configurations across 3 real healthcare datasets and 4x4 model combinations, plus targeted stress tests for high dimensionality, feature correlation, SNR, sample-size scaling, global calibration shift, and interaction misspecification.

Reasonably rigorous accompanying theory (estimation consistency under RSC assumptions, PFER/FDR control via knockoffs) with full proofs provided in the appendix, and the paper is forthright that exact support recovery is not claimed.

Two real-data case studies (COVID-19 Omicron shift, Lupus cross-ancestry gene expression) produce feature sets that are plausibly consistent with independently published clinical/genetic findings, offering some external face validity beyond the synthetic benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantees rest on a well-specification assumption (g(E_T[Y|X]) = h_S(X) + phi(X)^T delta) that is unlikely to hold exactly when h_S is itself a black-box model (SVM, gradient boosting) mismatched to the true generative process; the paper's own 'mismatched' experimental condition only partially probes this and still shows degraded performance, suggesting the theory's practical reach is limited.

The paper's own appendix (Table, Section E) shows that the knockoff-based FDR control -- the headline theoretical selling point of SGShift-K -- is empirically violated in several dense-shift settings (e.g., FDR up to 0.10-0.15 against an implied nominal target), undercutting confidence in the stated error-control guarantees under realistic conditions.

Real-world validation of selected features relies on post-hoc narrative agreement with the literature (COVID-19 and Lupus case studies) rather than any quantitative or statistically principled validation against known ground-truth shifted features; this is suggestive but weak evidence, and selectively reported examples cannot substitute for the semi-synthetic AUC comparisons that drive the paper's main performance claims.

Baseline methods (WhyShift, SHAP-based detector) were originally designed for different objectives (region discovery, distributional explanation-shift detection) and are adapted post-hoc by the authors into a feature-ranking AUC framework; this repurposing, acknowledged by the authors themselves, raises fairness concerns about the magnitude of the reported performance gap.

The method carries a substantial hyperparameter/design burden (link function, basis map including possible interaction terms, lambda schedules, absorption weighting c, knockoff aggregation strategy) whose joint sensitivity is only partially explored, making faithful reproduction and practical deployment nontrivial.

SGShift-A (absorption) is motivated primarily heuristically and its empirical advantage over plain SGShift is marginal across most reported settings (Table 1), raising the question of whether the added modeling complexity and extra theorem (3.2) are justified by the evidence.

Model-X knockoffs require accurate knowledge/estimation of the joint covariate distribution for valid construction; this assumption is non-trivial for real tabular data with mixed types and is not empirically interrogated in the real-data applications, where its violation would invalidate the FDR guarantees entirely.

The Impact Statement is entirely boilerplate and the main text lacks a dedicated limitations section discussing the practical risk of relying on a method whose formal guarantees are shown (in the appendix) to not hold reliably outside idealized settings.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reformulation of concept shift diagnosis as a sparse correction-learning problem rather than a plugin difference-of-estimators approach, which plausibly avoids the error-accumulation issue that the paper demonstrates empirically for baselines like WhyShift and Diff.

Solid theoretical contributions: consistency guarantees for the sparse correction under high-dimensional M-estimation assumptions (Theorems 3.1, 3.2) and a principled extension to false discovery control via Model-X knockoffs with both PFER and e-BH FDR guarantees (Theorem 3.3), including careful discussion of what is and is not claimed (e.g., exact support recovery is explicitly not claimed).

Extensive and thoughtfully designed experimental suite: semi-synthetic benchmarks across 3 real healthcare datasets with 16 model-pairing combinations each, dedicated stress tests for dense shift, high-dimensionality, feature correlation, SNR, sample-size scaling, global calibration shift, and interaction misspecification — this breadth substantially strengthens confidence that the method is robust rather than tuned to a narrow setting.

Consistent and often large performance gains over three reasonable baselines (Diff, an adapted WhyShift, and an adapted SHAP-based detector) across nearly all settings, with particularly notable robustness advantages in high-dimensional and small-sample regimes where baselines collapse.

Real-world validation goes beyond synthetic benchmarks: the COVID-19 Omicron case study and the Lupus cross-ancestry gene expression case study both recover findings independently corroborated by domain literature, lending external, substantive credibility to the method's practical utility.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility materials: datasets, preprocessing, and hyperparameters are documented in appendices, and sensitivity analyses for key tuning choices (penalty ranges, absorption weighting constant c) are reported.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees rely on fairly strong and somewhat idealized assumptions (correct model specification in Eq. 1, sub-Gaussian design, restricted strong convexity, independence of knockoff draws across repeats) that may not hold in the correlated, high-dimensional tabular settings the paper targets; the paper's own practical penalty-calibration heuristic (Appendix F) explicitly relies on an orthogonal-design approximation that departs from the general correlated-design theory, highlighting a gap between theory and the method actually deployed.

The knockoff construction for the GAM basis with interaction or nonlinear terms is acknowledged as an open methodological issue in the main text ("either a valid knockoff construction for the transformed design must be used, or statistics should be grouped at the raw-feature level") without being fully resolved; the interaction-shift experiment (Appendix K) is limited to one dataset and does not stress-test this concern much further.

Empirical FDR control for SGShift-K in Appendix E sometimes exceeds the nominal target under mismatched/dense conditions (e.g., 0.11–0.15 for Diabetes/SUPPORT2 mismatched dense settings against presumably lower nominal q), suggesting that the formal guarantees may be fragile outside well-behaved regimes, a point that is reported but not discussed critically in the main text.

Baseline comparisons (Diff, SHAP-based, WhyShift) are self-adapted implementations of methods not originally designed for this exact feature-attribution task, raising some question about whether the comparison is maximally fair/strong; stronger or more recent conditional-shift-specific baselines (e.g., Singh et al. 2024/2025, Zhang et al. 2023) are discussed in related work but not benchmarked empirically.

The paper's scope is restricted to tabular data with GAM-style additive corrections; extension to richer functional forms or non-tabular modalities is left as future work, limiting the generality of the immediate contribution.

The impact/ethics statement is minimal and generic, despite the paper directly dealing with sensitive attributes such as ancestry-based genetic differences and healthcare outcome disparities; a brief discussion of risks of misinterpreting or misusing such sparse attributions (e.g., overstating causal or biological interpretations from predictive feature selection) would have been appropriate given the real-data case studies presented.
